extracted.intended_audience: conference/workshop organizers, MER co-directors, mathematics educators, and education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evidence for organizing and evaluating special sessions, workshops, and banquets for mathematics-education audiences (attendance, pedagogy, format, networking, communications, and impacts). Emphasis on what makes sessions useful, well-attended, and effective for participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Session attendance/popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator of session popularity: room often nearly full; standing-room-only for late-comers signals that talks were popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMS arranges rooms anticipating audience size; crowded sessions are evidence of interest. Quantitative indicators used elsewhere include percent of constituencies attending (e.g., 'more than half of the mathematicians, 30% of the math-educators, and less than 20% of the K-12 survey respondents indicated they had attended a special session').

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic relevance and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain topics draw large crowds (e.g., ‘Introductory college mathematics: The critical filter for the majority’); other topics may attract fewer attendees depending on subject or time of day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose themes likely to interest target constituencies (K-12 vs post-secondary). Track which topics attract attendees to shape future programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical quality/modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Good pedagogy should be modeled in sessions; presenters ideally demonstrate teaching techniques rather than solely lecturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of good practice include hands-on laboratory components, interactive styles, and modeling cooperative learning. Anti-pattern: lecture-only presentations that 'did not model good pedagogy.' Several respondents wanted more modeling in afternoon breakout sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience engagement and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sessions should enable engagement (e.g., presenters engaging the audience in lengthy discussions; controversial talks producing lively debate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversial topics can provoke discussion; organizers should allow time/format for discussion. Evidence of success: standing-room-only crowds and extended audience dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering a forum for diverse/controversial views
rubrics_metrics.description: Special sessions should provide a forum for a range of views on educational reform without implying endorsement by organizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inviting controversial speakers (e.g., critique of NCTM Standards) can spark valuable community discussion; balance is needed since audience reaction may be strongly negative or positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness/impact to attendees
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether sessions were useful: learning new information, making personal contacts, and finding support for education activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey items used: extent sessions influenced decisions to attend meetings/workshops and self-reported usefulness categories ('Not at all', 'A little', 'Considerably', 'Very Much'). Majority who attended often reported sessions as useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking and professional contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Events should facilitate meeting people who share interests and exchanging ideas with professional peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banquet seating arranged for small-group discussion (round tables seating eight) and informal gatherings (cocktail hours, meals) were highlighted as important networking opportunities. Respondents cited networking as a primary benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banquet format effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Banquet as informal venue (no after-dinner speakers/themes) encourages small-group discussion and networking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of success: continued ticket sales, majority of attendees who attended would recommend the banquet. Consider cost accessibility for students (e.g., $45 fee may be too expensive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and accessibility considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Participant willingness to attend is sensitive to expense coverage; paying own transport/fees reduces likelihood of attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: nearly all would attend if expenses paid; attendance drops to slightly less than half if paying own transportation and conference fee; only 25-35% if paying all expenses. Banquet fee may deter grad students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications and dissemination effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: How MER 'spreads the word': word of mouth, newsletters, listservers, and electronic forwarding influence reach and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word of mouth is the most effective for recruitment; newsletters better for maintaining communications. Recommendations include expanding listservers and enabling easy forwarding of electronic posts to capitalize on word-of-mouth effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop program structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical workshop pattern: reception and keynote, morning panels (90 minutes), concurrent afternoon breakout sessions (90 minutes), Sunday reflections; panels include 2–4 speakers, breakouts limited in size (about 15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'standard' pattern was effective at sharing information while afternoon breakouts fostered more interaction. Organizers should design morning sessions to present breadth and afternoon sessions to deepen interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of lecture and interactive formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Need to balance lecture-oriented information sharing with interactive, participant-centered activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many participants preferred lecture to gather information in short time frames; others wanted more modeling of reform pedagogy. Suggested compromise: short presentations followed by structured discussion or reflection to engage participants while being efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakout session design and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Breakout sessions deliberately limited in size (generally ~15 participants) and designed to facilitate more interaction than morning panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sign-up control recommended. Afternoon sessions that used hands-on, interactive styles were singled out positively. Ensure breakouts build on morning panels' content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should include speakers whose individual presentations are well articulated with one another and represent a range of experiences and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels of 2–4 speakers lasting 90 minutes were generally effective; coherence among panelists improves information sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant composition and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally include a mix of university mathematics faculty, K–12 educators, education department members, and agency representatives to enrich perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Baton Rouge workshop had ~60.5% university math faculty, 22.3% K–12 educators, 9.2% education department members, and 5.3% agency staff. Inclusion of K–12 teachers was boosted by State Systemic Initiatives participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop topic selection and balance (K-12 vs undergraduate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track and select workshop themes across domains (general issues, direct K-12 connections, university issues, K-12 issues, systemic issues); adjust emphasis based on field needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis showed MER shifting emphasis from K-12 toward undergraduate issues; monitoring frequency and coverage of topics can guide future priorities (e.g., undergraduate curriculum/calculus reform frequency comparable to entire direct K-12 topic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methods and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use participant-observer methods and post-workshop surveys to gather data on attendance, perceived learning, intentions to apply ideas, pedagogical modeling, and satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys distributed on final morning (example response rate 47.4% at Baton Rouge). Use categorical response options for perceived influence and usefulness, and collect qualitative comments about pedagogy and intentions to implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of influence/intent to act
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether participants intend to incorporate workshop ideas into teaching, departmental practices, or to share with colleagues and administrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many respondents reported intentions to change or validate current practices and planned follow-up actions (colloquia, special meetings, informal sharing). Recognize institutional barriers to implementing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: pedagogical modeling vs information efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the trade-off between modeling interactive pedagogy (which takes time) and efficiently delivering a lot of information in limited workshop time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some participants argued lecture-discussion is most efficient for short workshops; others favored demonstration and practice. A suggested hybrid: brief presentation + structured small-group work/reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating/physical arrangements to facilitate discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange banquet and other meals with round tables seating ~8 to facilitate small-group discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This seating allowed small-group conversation to occupy the evening and was cited as meeting attendee needs; no after-dinner speakers amplified informal interaction.
